headline: November was dominated by Jensen Huang's ouster from Nvidia over an alleged Chinese spy affair and by Anthropic's record IPO, which pulled chip export controls and AI valuations into Washington politics. Underneath, enterprise AI spend and coding-agent use kept climbing while warnings about recursive self-improvement grew louder.

themes.title: Nvidia's leadership crisis and chip politics
themes.body: Jensen Huang admitted an affair with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, whom US intelligence suspects of being a Chinese spy, and was ousted as Nvidia CEO, with Colette Kress as interim CEO. NLW tracks the fallout: the Lutnick export-control reporting, bipartisan chip export bills in the lame duck session, a Commerce rule on remote chip access, Chinese reaction to new US export rules and the Nvidia board ruling out Huang's return. Former Biden advisors Ben Buchanan and Tantum Collins defend building a compute lead over China and spending it on safety.

themes.title: Anthropic goes public
themes.body: Anthropic proceeded with its IPO at falling valuations after the worst AI stock drawdown since 2020. NLW says Wall Street has no idea what it is worth, pointing to compute commitments including a troubled Lambda deal and a productivity suite aimed at Microsoft. On IPO day he ranked the ten biggest days in AI history, then covered the record $107 billion offering's aftermath. The AI:AM hosts discussed the amended S-1, and NLW highlights its language on approaching a recursive self-improvement danger threshold.

themes.title: Recursive self-improvement warnings
themes.body: METR's first independent safety report on Anthropic showed accelerating AI R&D, and an MIT paper showed GPT-6 Astra directly editing a smaller model's weights. Paul Christiano tells Dwarkesh there is a substantial chance of superintelligence within a year and that labs should pause algorithmic progress until security can stop weight theft. Bob McGrew counters that GPUs and wet labs make hard takeoff unlikely. Nathan Labenz's Bletchley Park keynote and Sentinel Bio's Joshua Monrad both argue for a pause, and Democratic calls for one are growing.

themes.title: Enterprise spend and AI-native operating models
themes.body: Menlo Ventures reports enterprise AI spend up nearly 5x per company, driven by agents, and Ramp, Databricks and Arcana Research data show token usage outpacing spend, more model switching and an Anthropic lead in enterprise. NLW distills seven habits of AI-native firms. Simon Willison tells Turing Post's Ksenia Se that coding agents have hit an inflection point yet made his work harder. Mihail Eric's Stanford course teaches agent-ready codebases. Scotiabank's Gautham Pallapa rethinks the SDLC in a risk-averse bank and Noblis CIO Mark Lay names four AI decisions.

themes.title: Model releases and the jagged frontier
themes.body: Anthropic's Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 set benchmark records, but NLW finds them jagged and notes many users still prefer Opus 5.5, which he calls a step change for agentic video. OpenAI's GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol drew harsh early reactions over coding regressions. Google released Gemini 4 Carbon and later Gemini 4 Neon, which NLW recommends for its different perspective. Simon Willison discusses how he evaluates models. Black Forest Labs presents FLUX 3 as one multimodal model, and Handshake AI explains how labs buy expert data.

themes.title: Designing products for agents
themes.body: Linear COO Cristina Cordova describes repositioning around agents after Karri Saarinen's 'issue tracking is dead' post, with an MCP server, an agent platform and usage-based pricing for AI features. Resend's Zeno Rocha serves agents through an 80-tool MCP server, a CLI and machine-readable pages. Cisco's Vijoy Pandey presents the open-source Scope observability platform and the Accord and Concord protocols for aligning enterprise agents. Simon Willison warns builders about the lethal trifecta and prompt injection, and Legora's Jacob Lauritzen runs evals without seeing confidential client data.

themes.title: AI for science and drug discovery
themes.body: Isomorphic Labs, which also raised new funding, is moving drug discovery onto computers; president Max Jaderberg cites AlphaFold as proof of concept and aims to replace animal toxicity testing. Helmholtz Munich's Fabian Theis treats virtual cells as perturbation-prediction world models and stresses baselines and metrics. Robinhood's Vlad Tenev argues math discovery from his startup Harmonic's Aristotle model should be decentralized rather than owned by labs, and Arda's Bob McGrew applies general robotics models to manufacturing with Anduril. Handshake AI's experts walk through the Vials life sciences benchmark.

themes.title: Midterms and data center politics
themes.body: NLW reads the 2026 midterm blue wave as having made data centers a campaign issue in California, Ohio, Texas, Georgia and Michigan, and predicts incremental federal AI rules and more state-level hurdles. He argues a post-midterm data center slowdown gives hyperscalers cover to trim CapEx, while Apple cut internal AI budgets. Buchanan and Collins see AI becoming an electoral issue, BallotBench's Brian Zhou joined AI:AM to discuss election-forecasting agents, and congressional hearings on chips are coming.

implications: Track compute supply as a political risk as well as a market one. Leadership changes at a dominant chip vendor, tighter export rules and remote-access restrictions can change compute pricing and availability with little notice.

Expect enterprise AI spend to keep rising as agents spread. Monitor token usage per workflow, plan for frequent model switching and negotiate contracts that do not lock you into one provider's pricing.

Design internal systems so agents are first-class users: documented APIs, MCP servers, CLIs and machine-readable documentation, plus observability that shows what agents did and why and defenses against prompt injection.

Do not choose models on launch benchmarks. New flagships arrive jagged, with regressions on some tasks, so keep task-level evaluations and let teams stay on older models where those still perform better.

Prepare governance for faster AI progress and stricter rules. Independent lab evaluations, pause proposals and state-level data center fights suggest controls on frontier systems and infrastructure could tighten quickly.
